text: The seven products in this experiment were prepared from nine traditional aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal, with Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar, included as the control. Each product was laid out in a completely randomised design with three replications and repeated over two years. The two years were analysed together as a pooled design, with year as a fixed effect and cultivar as a random effect. The model was Yijk = mu + Yi + Tj + (YT)ij + eijk, and the degrees of freedom were year 1, cultivar 9, year by cultivar 9, error 40 and total 59.

The results are set out in two parts. Part A covers the four cooked products, table rice, kichidi, pulao and payash, and Part B the three processed products, popped rice, puffed rice and flattened rice. Within each part every attribute is presented once for the group, with all the products of that part set together in one table and one figure, both giving the means pooled over the two years. Means were separated at the 5 per cent level and are reported with letter groupings; a cultivar is taken to differ from the control only where the two share no letter. Throughout, ** denotes significance at 1 per cent, * at 5 per cent and NS non-significance. Since a high value is favourable for some attributes and a low value for others, each cultivar is compared with the control in the direction appropriate to that attribute.

Each part closes with a composite quality score index, a check on the weights of that index using principal component analysis, a cluster analysis of the cultivar and product combinations, and a conclusion. Tables and figures are numbered continuously through both parts.

Discussion. Amylose content determines the firmness and separateness of the cooked grain. A higher content gives a firmer, drier grain that holds its shape, and a lower content a softer, stickier one. Amylose is laid down by granule bound starch synthase I at the Waxy locus, and cultivars differ in the allele they carry. Cooking disorganises the granule but does not alter the amount of amylose present.

Earlier work reports much the same. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found apparent amylose decides eating and processing behaviour; Tian et al. (2018) found crystallinity and digestibility fall without amylose changing; Cheng et al. (2019) found heat and moisture rebuild the matrix into a firmer gel; Devi and Badwaik (2022) found amylose explains most of the varietal difference in cooking. The most favourable entry differed between products. Kalojira and Tulaipanjii each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

Discussion. Starch is the energy supplying fraction of the grain and the basis of its texture. A higher value indicates a well filled endosperm and good recovery of the edible fraction. Starch content depends on how efficiently assimilate was moved into the endosperm during grain filling. In the prepared product it is further affected by the loss of low molecular weight material and by the water taken up in cooking.

This is consistent with previous studies. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found starch makes up about nine tenths of milled rice by dry weight; Tian et al. (2018) found the residual starch is swollen and less crystalline; Iqbal et al. (2021) found restructured starch resists digestion; Cheng et al. (2019) found how far the starch gelatinises drives texture and digestion. The leading cultivar changed with the product, Kalonunia, Kataribhog, Lal Badshabhog and Radhunipagal ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Discussion. Protein is the main nutritional contribution of rice after energy, and it also firms the cooked grain through disulphide bonding. Most of the protein is glutelin stored in protein bodies beneath the aleurone, and the amount depends on the nitrogen moved into the grain during filling. Cooking does not alter it.

Published work points in the same direction. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found total protein is unchanged by hydrothermal treatment; Cheng et al. (2019) found disulphide cross links raise firmness; Akter et al. (2025) found protein rose from 6.68 to 9.42 per cent after treatment; Iqbal et al. (2021) found the protein network controls enzyme access to starch. The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalojira, Kalonunia and Radhunipagal, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Discussion. Soluble protein is the fraction that remains extractable, and therefore digestible, after cooking. A higher value indicates that heat has not aggregated the protein. Heat ruptures the protein bodies and then cross links the released chains through disulphide bonds, which lowers the extractable fraction. Cultivars richer in cysteine lose more.

The same pattern has been reported before. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found solubility changes while total protein does not; Cheng et al. (2019) found cross linking lowers the extractable fraction; Kabir et al. (2025) found treatment changes how protein and bound phenolics associate; Roy et al. (2019) found solubility falls as steam and soaking get harsher. Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Tulaipanjii each headed the ranking in a different product, so this attribute cannot settle the selection for the group as a whole.

Discussion. Lipid is located in the germ and aleurone and carries the fat soluble vitamins and the aroma compounds. A higher content is better, subject to the fact that excess lipid shortens shelf life. Lipid is stored as triacylglycerol in the germ and aleurone, so the value reflects both the size of these tissues in the cultivar and the extent of milling.

Earlier reports support this finding. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found lipid sits in germ and aleurone and oxidises readily; Hu et al. (2019) found moving water inside the kernel shifts the lipid bearing tissues; Devi and Badwaik (2022) found traditional cultivars differ widely in proximate composition; Oliveira et al. (2026) found milling is the main route by which the outer layers are lost. No single cultivar was superior in all the products. Dudeshwar, Kalojira and Radhunipagal ranked highest in different ones, so the decision depends on the product concerned.

Discussion. Ash is the residue remaining after ignition and represents the total inorganic contribution of the grain. Ash follows the germ and aleurone, which carry most of the mineral matter, so cultivars with a thicker aleurone or a larger embryo give higher values.

Similar results have been published elsewhere. Hu et al. (2019) found ash follows how much germ and aleurone survive; Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found the spread in ash comes from the outer grain layers; Jannasch and Wang (2020) found the steeping medium can add to the mineral fraction; Kumar et al. (2022) found ash is redistributed rather than lost on treatment. Dudeshwar gave the most favourable value in every product of this group, and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.

Discussion. Phenolic acids are the principal antioxidants of the grain and are largely bound to the pericarp cell wall. A higher retained content in the product is better. Most phenolic acid is bound to arabinoxylan in the pericarp wall. Heat cleaves these bonds and releases it, while simultaneously degrading and leaching the free fraction, so the value recorded is the balance of the two.

Comparable observations appear in the literature. Phimphilai et al. (2026) found popping and steam cooking cut total phenolics sharply; Shavandi et al. (2023) found infrared puffing raises the extractable fraction; Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found heat frees ferulic and p-coumaric acid from the cell wall; Kabir et al. (2025) found soaking and cooking lower phenolic acids, bound exceeding free. The leading cultivar changed with the product, Kalonunia, Kataribhog and Lal Badshabhog ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Discussion. Flavonoids contribute to antioxidant activity and to pericarp colour. They degrade readily on heating, so the residual content indicates how gently the grain was treated. Flavonoids are synthesised in the pericarp and cultivars differ in the amount deposited. They are readily destroyed by heat, so the residual content reflects both the initial level and the treatment.

Previous studies describe the same behaviour. Phimphilai et al. (2026) found flavonoids break down more readily than total phenolics; Kabir et al. (2025) found most flavonoid sits in the bound fraction; Oliveira et al. (2026) found long cooking can cost up to forty per cent; Devi and Badwaik (2022) found traditional cultivars differ several fold. The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalonunia and Kataribhog, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Discussion. Antioxidant capacity measures the activity of the whole bioactive fraction rather than its quantity, so a higher value is desirable. Antioxidant capacity derives from the surviving phenolics and flavonoids together with browning products formed during heating, so cultivars rich in bound phenolics retain more of it.

Earlier work reports much the same. Phimphilai et al. (2026) found capacity tracks phenolic and flavonoid content; Shavandi et al. (2023) found activity moves with total phenolics as puffing changes; Kabir et al. (2025) found the bound phenolics account for most of the activity; Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found browning products add to measured activity. Kalonunia, Kataribhog, Lal Badshabhog and Radhunipagal each headed the ranking in a different product, so this attribute cannot settle the selection for the group as a whole.

Discussion. Phytic acid binds iron, zinc and calcium in the intestine and prevents their absorption. A lower content is therefore better, since it releases the very minerals the grain supplies. Phytate is deposited as globoids in the aleurone during grain filling and is hydrolysed by endogenous phytase during soaking, so the residue depends on both processes.

This is consistent with previous studies. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found treated brown rice holds about half the phytate of untreated; Kumar et al. (2022) found less phytate means more iron and zinc absorbed; Bhar et al. (2022) found cutting phytate is a main nutritional argument for processed grain; Hu et al. (2019) found germination and hydrothermal treatment work in different ways. No single cultivar was superior in all the products. Dudeshwar, Gobindabhog and Kalonunia ranked highest in different ones, so the decision depends on the product concerned.

Discussion. Copper is required for iron transport and for several enzymes, and cereals are a principal dietary source. A higher content in the product is better. Copper is carried into the grain by COPT and HMA transporters and stored mainly in the aleurone, so cultivars with greater uptake and translocation accumulate more.

Published work points in the same direction. Sonu et al. (2025) found genotype governs grain micronutrient concentration; Kumar et al. (2022) found trace metals shift between bran and endosperm rather than being lost; Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found soluble minerals move inward from husk and pericarp; Hu et al. (2019) found water moving inside the kernel displaces elements from the aleurone. The most favourable entry differed between products. Dudeshwar, Harinakhuri and Radhatilak each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

Discussion. Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional disorder in rice eating populations, so the iron retained in the product is of direct importance. A higher content is better. Grain iron depends on the amount remobilised from the flag leaf and on the chelators that transport it, both of which differ between cultivars. Cooking moves some of it inward from the pericarp.

The same pattern has been reported before. Sonu et al. (2025) found grain iron is heritable but few lines reach nutritional targets; Kumar et al. (2022) found iron moves inward and becomes more available; Jannasch and Wang (2020) found the steep water can carry iron and calcium into the endosperm; Akter et al. (2025) found iron fell while protein and zinc were concentrated. The leading cultivar changed with the product, Kalojira and Kalonunia ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Discussion. Zinc is required for immunity, growth and wound healing, and is the mineral after iron most often deficient in rice based diets. A higher content is better. Zinc loading depends on the HMA2 and HMA4 transporters and on remobilisation during grain filling. It is held in the aleurone largely as phytate salts.

Earlier reports support this finding. Kumar et al. (2022) found zinc moves outward on treatment, unlike iron; Sonu et al. (2025) found grain zinc is polygenic with wide genotypic variance; Hu et al. (2019) found zinc is held in the germ and aleurone; Oliveira et al. (2026) found polishing matters more than the thermal step. The leading position was shared between Kalojira, Kalonunia, Radhatilak and Tulaipanjii, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Discussion. Manganese is required by superoxide dismutase and certain other enzymes. The dietary requirement is small but cereals supply most of it, so a higher content is better. Manganese enters through NRAMP and MTP transporters and accumulates in the aleurone, so the value depends on uptake and on how much of the outer grain survives milling.

Similar results have been published elsewhere. Hu et al. (2019) found aleurone bound elements are displaced as water redistributes; Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found soluble minerals migrate inward during steeping; Sonu et al. (2025) found genotype counts for more than environment in mineral density; Kumar et al. (2022) found retention depends on the starting level and the treatment. Dudeshwar, Kataribhog and Radhatilak each headed the ranking in a different product, so this attribute cannot settle the selection for the group as a whole.

Discussion. Lightness measures how pale the product has remained. It falls with browning and with inward movement of pigments, so a higher value generally indicates gentler processing. Lightness falls as browning products accumulate and as pericarp pigments dissolve and migrate inward. Cultivars with more reducing sugar and free amino nitrogen brown further under the same treatment.

Comparable observations appear in the literature. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found darkening comes from pigment movement and browning; Srisang et al. Discussion. Appearance governs the first impression and therefore whether the product is tried at all. Appearance follows the colour coordinates, which are determined by pigment migration and browning, so the cultivars that remain pale head the ranking.

Earlier reports support this finding. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found colour is among the two attributes that most limit acceptance; Dutta and Mahanta (2014) found appearance caps the market whatever the nutritional merit; Srisang et al. (2021) found harder processing gives a visibly darker product; Akter et al. (2025) found a darker product was nonetheless more acceptable overall. The most favourable entry differed between products. Discussion. Consistency describes the textural coherence of the finished dish and how well it matches what the preparation requires. Consistency depends on the degree of starch gelatinisation and subsequent retrogradation, and on the protein network surrounding the granules.

Similar results have been published elsewhere. Cheng et al. (2019) found heat and moisture give a firmer, less sticky network; Iqbal et al. Discussion. Cooking quality summarises water uptake, cooking time and the structural integrity of the cooked grain. Cooking quality depends on gelatinisation temperature, amylose content and the structural integrity of the grain, which is why it tracks alkali spreading value and amylose.

Comparable observations appear in the literature. Ayamdoo et al. The leading position was shared between Dudeshwar, Gobindabhog and Harinakhuri, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

The analysis of variance answers one attribute at a time, so a single figure was needed to establish which cultivar is best overall. text: Seven traditional products were prepared from nine aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal together with Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar used as the control. Four of the products are cooked, namely table rice, kichidi, pulao and payash, and three are processed, namely popped rice, puffed rice and flattened rice. Each was laid out in a completely randomised design with three replications and repeated over two years, the two years being analysed together as a pooled design. Between 22 and 25 quality attributes were determined in each product, covering the nutritional, bioactive, mineral, colour and sensory groups, giving 162 attribute and product combinations in all.

The cultivar effect was significant in 157 of the 162 combinations, that is 96.9 per cent. The year effect was significant in 68 (42.0 per cent) and the year by cultivar interaction in 49 (30.2 per cent). The margin between these three figures is the central result of the experiment. Almost every attribute separated the cultivars, fewer than half separated the years, and fewer than a third showed the cultivar differences changing in size between years. The identity of the cultivar therefore governs the quality of the finished product, the year of production has a smaller and less consistent effect, and the ranking of the cultivars is largely stable from one year to the next. In practical terms a cultivar chosen on one year of data can be expected to hold its position in the following year.

Coefficients of variation were low throughout, which shows that the trials were well controlled and that the differences reported are not an artefact of experimental error. Table B sets out the position for each product separately.

Because the analysis of variance answers one attribute at a time, and because a high value is favourable for some attributes and a low value for others, a single figure was needed to rank the cultivars overall. This was obtained by the total quality scoring approach of Ismail et al. (2001), whose validity as a measure of overall quality was later examined by Kraggerud et al. (2012). Every attribute on which the cultivars differed significantly was scored from 0 to 100 in the favourable direction, averaged within the five groups, and combined by weight, sensory carrying 30 per cent, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10.

On this index the best cultivar was Gobindabhog for payash and popped rice; Kalojira for table rice; Radhunipagal for kichidi; Kataribhog for pulao; Radhatilak for puffed rice; Harinakhuri for flattened rice. No single cultivar was best for all seven products, so the choice of raw material must follow the product intended. Kalojira appeared among the first three in four products and Gobindabhog, Kalonunia and Radhatilak in three each, so these four are the entries of widest usefulness across the group.

The control ranked last of the ten entries in six of the seven products and ninth in the seventh. The margin between the best cultivar and the control ranged from 16.5 points in puffed rice to 45.7 in payash. Replacing Dudeshwar with the cultivars named here would therefore raise the quality of every product appreciably, and would do so without any change in the method of preparation.
How far the ranking can be relied upon

The weights used in the index were chosen rather than calculated, and the ranking was therefore checked against a second set of weights derived from the data. Principal component analysis was applied to the merit scores, and each attribute was weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading times the share of variance that component carries. Taking the seven products together, the mean rank correlation between the two rankings was 0.946, the lowest was 0.867, and the same cultivar came first in 6 of the seven. The ranking is therefore a property of the data and not of the weights adopted. Where the two disagreed, the cultivars concerned were close together on the index in any case.

A second and quite independent check is provided by the count of attributes on which each cultivar exceeded the control, which uses no weights at all. The cultivar with the best net balance was the same as the cultivar with the highest index in three of the seven products, and in the remainder the two entries were again close on the index. Taken together, the two checks show that the recommendations do not depend on the particular scheme by which the index was constructed.

It should be noted that principal component analysis is used here only to set the weights. The components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, because a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the better one.

Cluster analysis was run on all 70 cultivar and product combinations across the two parts, using the attributes measured in every product of each part. Ward's method gave 7 groups, of which 5 contained a single product only. The clusters therefore correspond to products rather than to cultivars. When one preparation is compared with another it is the method of preparation, not the cultivar, that determines the broad quality type; within any one preparation the cultivar is the variable under the control of the processor. The two findings are complementary rather than contradictory. The preparation fixes the type of product and the cultivar fixes its standing within that type.

The quality of these seven traditional products is determined principally by the cultivar from which they are made. Nine of the ten entries tested were superior to the non-aromatic control, and for each product a specific cultivar can be recommended: Gobindabhog for payash and popped rice; Kalojira for table rice; Radhunipagal for kichidi; Kataribhog for pulao; Radhatilak for puffed rice; Harinakhuri for flattened rice. These recommendations rest on a composite quality score index that has been shown to be insensitive to the weights used and to agree with an unweighted count against the control. Where a processor makes more than one of these products, Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Kalonunia and Radhatilak are the entries that perform well across the widest range.

Three qualifications should be stated. First, the index ranks these ten entries relative to one another and is not an absolute scale, so it would have to be recomputed if further cultivars were added. Second, the trials covered two years at one location, and confirmation over more years and more sites is needed before any general recommendation is issued. Third, the weights placed on the five attribute groups reflect a judgement about their relative importance, and a processor whose market rests chiefly on one aspect of quality would be right to recompute the index under weights of their own.

For breeding work directed at improving this group of cultivars, parents are best drawn from different clusters, since crosses between distant clusters are the more likely to release useful variation. The cultivars identified here also merit testing in products beyond the seven examined, since the cluster analysis indicates that each preparation makes its own demands of the raw material.
